meta.title: Pricing and Timelines for Software and AI Projects
meta.description: Genixo's starting offers, what drives the cost of software and AI projects, the costs often forgotten, and how to estimate payback before you start.

hero.title: What a project costs, and what decides the cost
hero.lead: Every project starts with a small, scoped first step. Below are those steps, the factors that move the price and the costs that proposals often leave out.

answer.label: In short
answer.text: Genixo work starts with a scoped first step: an AI readiness assessment, a fixed-scope AI pilot, a discovery sprint for custom software, a product discovery workshop, or an NGSD intro. The final cost of a project depends mainly on integrations, the condition of your data, accuracy requirements and where the system runs.

sections.label: What drives cost
sections.title: Six factors that move the price

items.title: Integrations
items.text: Each system the solution has to read from or write to, such as an ERP, CRM, e-invoice or telephony system, adds work and testing.

items.title: Condition of your data
items.text: Clean, structured data is cheaper to work with than scanned documents, duplicates or inconsistent codes.

items.title: Accuracy requirements
items.text: The higher the required accuracy, the larger the test set, the more review steps and the longer the pilot.

items.title: Where the system runs
items.text: Running models on your servers needs suitable hardware. Using an API provider has no hardware cost but has usage fees and KVKK consequences.

items.title: Users and permissions
items.text: Many roles, approval chains and document-level permissions take more design and testing.

items.title: Support after launch
items.text: Monitoring, fixes and improvements after go-live are part of the real cost. [[TODO-033]]

sections.label: Estimating payback
sections.title: How to estimate payback before you start
sections.lead: An illustrative method, not a promise. In a pilot, the inputs are replaced with measured values.
paragraphs: Monthly benefit = hours saved per month × fully loaded hourly cost + cost of errors avoided per month − monthly running costs.
Payback period = one-off cost ÷ monthly benefit.
Total cost of ownership over three years = one-off cost + 36 × monthly running costs, including the forgotten costs listed above.
If the monthly benefit is small or uncertain, the right next step is a measurement, not a build.

sections.label: Public support
sections.title: KOSGEB and other support programmes
paragraphs: KOSGEB runs programmes that support SMEs' digital transformation. Programme scope, eligible sectors and limits change over time, and many small software projects fall outside them. We check the current official conditions with you before suggesting that a programme applies. [[TODO-071]]

items.q: Why don't you publish a fixed price per project?
items.a: Because two projects with the same name can differ several times in integrations, data condition and accuracy requirements. The first steps above have published terms; the build is quoted after scope is defined.
